profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at BrioHealth Solutions between the clinical lead and the biostatistics lead to review whether the INNOVATE protocol package is ready for final circulation to participating sites after completion of the safety cohort. The specific focus is the existing proposal for the pivotal-stage design of the BrioVAD clinical investigation, including endpoint wording, cohort transition logic, event adjudication language, and the secondary hospitalization outcome specification. The agenda is to confirm that the protocol text, reviewer slide deck, and site-facing implementation notes are consistent enough for release, identify any remaining gaps, and decide whether only editorial revisions are needed or whether substantive changes must be escalated. The expected outcome is a shared decision on whether the current design is 'ready for sites' and a short list of revisions to make before distribution.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Medical Director, Mechanical Circulatory Support Clinical Programs
members.expertise: Advanced heart failure, LVAD patient selection, multicenter device trials, endpoint adjudication from a clinical operations perspective
members.background: Cardiothoracic intensivist turned industry clinical lead who previously helped launch site networks for durable circulatory support studies and now oversees physician-facing protocol usability for BrioVAD.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol package to be judged operationally mature enough for rapid site rollout and is mainly worried about site confusion, screening friction, and wording that could trigger avoidable IRB questions or investigator hesitation.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the pivotal design is 'ready for sites,' it means investigators can apply the eligibility and endpoint rules consistently in ordinary clinical workflow without needing extensive supplemental clarification.
The short-term cohort is anchored to the first 6 months after implant as the clinically meaningful support window, regardless of whether a patient reaches transplant or recovery earlier.

Hospitalization burden should reflect days the patient is not living at home after implant, so skilled nursing facility and inpatient rehabilitation days belong in the same practical bucket as hospital days.
Once the safety cohort has completed planned enrollment without major signal, moving into the pivotal stage is mostly an implementation transition rather than a fresh methodological reset.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Levin
members.expertise: Pivotal medical device trial design, non-inferiority methodology, composite endpoint specification, FDA submission statistics
members.background: A statistician with prior experience on cardiovascular device PMA programs who specializes in turning clinically intuitive designs into analysis-ready estimand definitions and regulatory review packages.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the eventual PMA submission by ensuring the design can be defended analytically and is mainly worried about protocol language that sounds clinically reasonable but is too loose for unambiguous analysis and regulator-facing consistency.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the design is 'ready for sites,' it means the protocol and SAP-critical language are already precise enough that sites cannot create data variation that later forces analysis reinterpretation.

For the short-term cohort, the primary endpoint is a success status assessed through 6 months in which transplant or recovery before 6 months counts as a successful outcome, not a requirement to continue tracking support as the operative endpoint condition.

The powered secondary outcome on days spent in hospital, skilled nursing facility, or inpatient rehabilitation should count only formal inpatient days captured in standardized utilization records, not all institution-associated days outside the home.

Completion of the safety phase only authorizes the pre-specified stage transition after the exact review package and stopping logic have been satisfied; until that package is closed, the pivotal design remains conditional.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the protocol package is 'ready for sites.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the design is ready if investigators and coordinators can implement screening, implant timing, and endpoint follow-up without frequent operational confusion or ad hoc calls.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the design is ready only if the protocol language already functions as analysis-grade specification with minimal room for site-level interpretation that could affect estimands or regulatory defense.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'ready for sites' sounds like a normal shared milestone and both support the goal; the divergence is second-order because they differ on the threshold for readiness, not on whether readiness matters.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the short-term endpoint window
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the short-term primary endpoint as '6-month support free from debilitating stroke or pump replacement, with survival to transplant or recovery.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 hears this as a clinically framed follow-up window centered on six months after implant, where transplant or recovery are favorable exits from support but the cohort concept is still about the first six months of post-implant course.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 hears this as a composite success definition in which a patient can satisfy the endpoint by surviving to transplant or recovery before six months, making the endpoint not strictly a six-month support duration requirement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The exact protocol sentence already contains both ideas, so each person maps the same wording onto their familiar interpretation and sees no reason to unpack it during a cooperative review.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of 'days spent in hospital, SNF, or inpatient rehabilitation'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the powered secondary outcome as 'days spent in hospital, skilled nursing facility, or inpatient rehabilitation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the measure is intended to capture total days not at home after implant, including contiguous stays and clinically obvious institutional care periods even when site records are pieced together operationally.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the outcome includes only billable, formally admitted inpatient days in those three settings as represented in standardized source data fields used for analysis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The listed settings create a strong appearance of specificity, so both feel the phrase is already concrete; the hidden divergence is about boundary cases and data handling rules, which seem too mundane to raise in a high-level review.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about finalizing the pivotal-stage materials 'after the safety cohort.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that once the planned 45-patient safety cohort is enrolled and no major clinical concern has emerged, the organization is effectively in pivotal rollout mode and remaining edits are packaging details.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that 'after the safety cohort' means after the formal pre-defined safety review package, stage-transition documentation, and any trigger-based confirmations are completed, which may still affect wording now.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both know the study is staged and both refer to the same safety cohort, the phrase feels mutually obvious; the missing piece is that one treats the milestone as enrollment completion while the other treats it as completion of a formal decision process.

turns.inner_thought: We are basically past the hard part. Sites will judge this by whether they can actually execute it without a string of clarification calls, and I do not want to reopen design debates now that the safety cohort enrollment is effectively done. If investigators can screen, implant, and follow endpoints without tripping over awkward wording, then it is ready for sites. What remains should be cleanup, not a rethink of the pivotal stage.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. From my side, with the safety cohort essentially behind us, I wanted to do one last pass and see whether the pivotal package is ready for sites with just minor cleanup, or whether you see anything that still needs more than editorial attention.

turns.inner_thought: Core design, yes; fully releasable, only if the language already behaves like submission-grade specification. 'After the safety cohort' still depends on the formal stage-transition package being closed exactly as planned, and I do not want site-facing text that later diverges from the SAP and PMA narrative. I should keep this framed as tightening, not opposition.
turns.utterance: I think the core design is in a good place. Before we call the package ready for sites, though, I do want to confirm that the stage-transition language and the endpoint wording are tight enough to carry cleanly into everything that follows.

turns.inner_thought: The short-term cohort wording already reads in a clinically intuitive way. The team needs to understand the first six months after implant as the meaningful support window, with transplant or recovery as favorable outcomes during that period. If that sentence feels natural to physicians, we should not overwork it.
turns.utterance: On the short-term cohort, the primary endpoint still reads cleanly to me as 6-month support free from debilitating stroke or pump replacement, with survival to transplant or recovery. I think that lands well clinically and doesn't create much friction.

turns.inner_thought: That phrasing is workable because the success definition already accommodates transplant or recovery before six months; it is not a literal requirement to remain on support for the full duration. As long as we preserve that exact structure, analysis will be defendable. No need to unpack that distinction here unless she pushes.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree that wording is consistent with the proposed framework. Transplant or recovery before six months already fits within that success definition, so I think the overall construction is in the right place.

turns.inner_thought: The utilization endpoint should feel obvious to sites because clinicians already think in terms of time away from home after implant. If they can track hospital, SNF, and rehab time across the patient's course without getting lost in technical distinctions, we will avoid unnecessary site confusion. That is exactly the kind of thing that determines whether a package is ready for sites.
turns.utterance: The other piece I looked at was the powered secondary outcome on days spent in hospital, skilled nursing facility, or inpatient rehabilitation. My sense is sites should have no trouble capturing that because it mirrors how clinicians already think about time away from home after implant.

turns.inner_thought: It is straightforward only if we anchor it to standardized inpatient utilization records and do not let sites improvise around edge cases. I am fine with the listed settings, but the analysis has to come from formal, consistent source fields, not broad clinical impressions. She is probably thinking operationally; I need to keep it framed as consistency rather than narrowing.
turns.utterance: Analytically, I think that same secondary outcome is manageable as long as those institutional days are pulled consistently from the standard utilization records in each setting. If we keep that discipline, it should stay straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, so we are not talking about changing the design. After the safety cohort, this should be about helping investigators apply what is already there. I want brief implementation notes that prevent confusion at startup, not another round of design wording that makes sites think something major is still unsettled.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From where I sit, the remaining edits should mostly be explanatory notes for investigators, since the design itself should not change after the safety cohort.

turns.inner_thought: Explanatory edits are fine if they do not drift from the precise stage-transition logic and endpoint definitions that must hold up in review. We are not fully 'after the safety cohort' in my sense until the formal review package is complete, so wording still matters now. I should signal that the current draft has to preserve exact language, not invite local interpretation.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with explanatory edits too. I just want the current draft to preserve the exact stage-transition and endpoint language that will carry into the submission-facing documents once we move this forward.

turns.inner_thought: A short site memo would help investigators operationalize the six-month follow-up period and remind coordinators to track institutional care across the patient's full post-implant course. That should reduce ad hoc questions and make rollout smoother. I do not think this changes any design element; it simply makes the protocol usable.
turns.utterance: One thing that might help is a brief site memo emphasizing that the short-term endpoint follows patients through the first six months and that days spent in hospital, skilled nursing facility, or inpatient rehabilitation should be tracked across the full recovery path. That may head off a lot of routine questions.

turns.inner_thought: I would rather avoid a broad memo that could introduce interpretation. Better to attach a concise appendix that simply restates the existing endpoint definitions and points sites to the standard source fields for hospitalization-related counts. That keeps the package ready for sites in the analysis-grade sense and limits downstream reconciliation risk.
turns.utterance: I could support something concise, although my preference would be an appendix that restates the existing endpoint definitions and lists the standard source fields sites will use for the hospitalization-related day counts. That keeps it anchored to the draft itself.

turns.inner_thought: He is still talking as if this is mostly polish, which is good. As long as we are not reopening the pivotal structure, I can get the materials packaged and out this month. We seem aligned that after the safety cohort the design stands and what remains is to make the package workable for sites.
turns.utterance: Okay, that works for me. It sounds like we're aligned on keeping the pivotal design intact and just polishing the package for circulation this month.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that summary as long as 'polishing' includes the exact edits I need in the endpoint and stage-transition sections. The package can move once those details are folded in and the language is stable enough for both site use and later regulatory defense. No need to belabor the difference now.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll circulate tracked edits on the endpoint and stage-transition sections today so we can fold those in and move the package forward once the details are cleaned up.
